findings.summary: The decimal-to-binary division process is flattened into alternating one-line fragments instead of a table or diagram.
findings.fix: Show the conversion as a table with columns Step | Quotient | Remainder, then read the remainders bottom-up to get 1101.

findings.summary: The 'Hex' section repeats the hex table without adding anything new, and its one-idea summary is split across two ideas in one prose sentence.
findings.evidence: All three languages write hex with 0x. Each hex digit is exactly 4 bits, so convert by grouping.
findings.fix: Fold into section 2 as two bullets: 'Hex literal is 0x in all three languages' and 'One hex digit = 4 bits, convert by grouping'.

findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "multiplies", "division").
findings.evidence: Left shift x << k multiplies by 2^k; right shift x >> k floors division by 2^k, and >>> (Java/JS) fills zeros while >> keeps the sign bit
findings.fix: Add the point with an explanation and an example.

findings.summary: The NOT section shows code before its idea is explained and omits OR/NOT identities consistently; the bitwise table also lacks a NOT/shift visual for sign behaviour.
findings.evidence:
python
print(~5, ~5 & 0xFF)
~5 = -6; the mask keeps the low 8 bits
findings.fix: State the rule (~x = -x - 1, mask keeps low 8 bits) first, then show the code as a confirming example.

findings.summary: Right shift row says it 'keeps the sign bit' while the Java/JS row is labelled separately, but Python/C behavior of >> on negatives is not stated, and the example is a prose callout.
findings.evidence: x >> k | floor of x / 2^k | keeps the sign bit
findings.fix: Label the row 'arithmetic shift (sign-extends)' and put -7 >> 1 = -4 in the table or a one-line bullet.

findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "subtraction", "addition").
findings.evidence: Addition and subtraction use the same hardware for signed and unsigned values, which is why this encoding is used
findings.fix: Add the point with an explanation and an example.

findings.summary: The claim that left-shifting a signed int into the sign bit is undefined in C/C++ is outdated for C++.
findings.evidence: Left-shifting a signed int into the sign bit is undefined in C/C++
findings.fix: Say it is undefined in C. In C++ it has been defined since C++14 when the result is representable, and C++20 defines it as two's-complement wraparound. Overflowing shifts, such as shifting past the width or shifting a negative value in C, are still undefined or implementation-specific.

findings.summary: Several bullets hold two ideas, and the sign-bit example is compressed into a single equation.
findings.evidence:
abs(INT_MIN) overflows: +2^(n-1) does not fit
Signed and unsigned share the same adder for + and -
findings.fix: Split the bullets; add a small table of 8-bit patterns (0111 1111=127, 1000 0000=-128, 1111 1111=-1).

findings.summary: The x & (x-1) step is shown as three stacked fragments rather than a aligned bit diagram, and the 'Parenthesize' callout holds two ideas.
findings.fix: Render as a three-row aligned table or code block; split the callout into a precedence rule and the fix.

findings.summary: The mistakes section states the precedence rule inconsistently: the bullet says '==' binds tighter than '&' and also lists '!=' only in the callout.
findings.fix: Add a single bullet: 'In C, C++, Java, == and != bind tighter than &; always parenthesize the masked part'.

findings.summary: The only worked example under 'Single number' has two unpaired values, so it never shows the lone value surviving.
findings.evidence: "Single number: XOR all elements, pairs cancel" / "Lone value left: O(n) time, O(1) space" / "1^2^1^3^2^5 = 3^5 = 011^101 = 110 = 6"
findings.fix: Use an array with one unpaired value (e.g. 1^2^1^3^2 = 3) to show the single-number trick. Keep the two-unpaired case as a separate warning example.

findings.summary: The XOR example line packs the whole computation, and the two-unpaired-values bullet leaves a gap with no answer to how to separate them.
findings.evidence: Two unpaired values: XOR is their combination, not either one
findings.fix: Split the example into steps (pairs cancel, left 3^5 = 6) and either state how to separate the two values or say it is out of scope.

findings.summary: Counting-bits section places the DP bullet with two formulas in one bullet and the code appears after the list without a leading idea sentence.
findings.evidence:
DP for 0..n: bits[i] = bits[i >> 1] + (i & 1)
Or bits[i & (i-1)] + 1, O(n)
findings.fix: Make each recurrence its own bullet, with its meaning (drop last bit / drop lowest set bit).

findings.summary: The section does not cover an outline point (missing "identities", "kernighan").
findings.evidence: XOR identities: x^x=0, x^0=x; single number is a fold of XOR; Kernighan counts bits in O(set bits)
findings.fix: Add the point with an explanation and an example.

findings.summary: The cheat sheet states the shift rows as '<< multiply by 2^k' / '>> divide by 2^k (floor)' without the overflow/sign caveats, and 'Traps' is a prose run-on holding three ideas.
findings.evidence: Write (x&1)==0: == binds tighter than &. Use 1L<<i for 64-bit. In Python, mask negatives: x & 0xFFFFFFFF.
findings.fix: Turn the Traps line into three one-line bullets.

findings.summary: The cheat sheet's power-of-two trick is written differently from page 4, mixing '!(x&(x-1))' with '(x & (x-1)) == 0'.
findings.fix: Use the same form on both pages.
